paragraphs: Artemis investigates why adding intermediate reasoning can hurt visual perception. The authors argue that the representation of reasoning matters: free-form language describes meaning, while perception requires keeping track of objects and their spatial locations. Their approach makes those visual states explicit throughout the reasoning process.

Each intermediate step consists of an object label and a bounding box. This gives the model a concrete proposal that can be checked and supervised directly. A chain of these proposals records how the model progresses through the image, reducing the ambiguity of verbal descriptions. The method builds perception policies around a spatial, object-centered chain rule and uses one architecture across different perceptual tasks.

The model is trained with grounding and detection examples from natural images and generalizes to counting and geometric perception tasks. These findings support structured visual reasoning as a useful basis for broader perception policies. The contribution is both a way to represent intermediate decisions and a way to make their quality directly assessable during learning.
icml-2026-artemis-structured-visual-reas.tldr: Artemis represents visual reasoning as sequences of object labels and bounding boxes, supporting perception policies that generalize across tasks.

paragraphs: Optimization modeling requires a model to turn a problem into a mathematical formulation, write and run solver code, inspect the result, and revise its solution. The authors find that training reasoning models on complete, prewritten solutions can help easier problems while damaging performance on harder ones. They suggest this supervision can interfere with the model’s existing problem-solving process.

CALM instead lets the base model begin its own solution. At the first detected error, it adds a brief corrective hint and allows generation to continue. These interventions change fewer than 2.6% of generated tokens. The repaired solutions then support supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning.

The resulting 4B model, STORM, achieves 68.9% macro-average accuracy across five benchmarks, matching 671B DeepSeek-R1-0528. A matched control on hard benchmarks also favors CALM over learning from complete solutions supplied by stronger teachers. For this task, the results support local correction as a more effective training signal than replacing the model’s entire solution.
icml-2026-calm-before-the-storm-unlockin.tldr: CALM trains optimization models by briefly correcting their own solutions, producing a 4B specialist that matches a much larger model on five benchmarks.

paragraphs: Generalized category discovery asks a model to assign unlabeled examples to either familiar categories or newly discovered ones. CoGe-GCD approaches this as a problem of composition: familiar visual building blocks may appear in unfamiliar combinations that indicate a new category. The authors identify unstructured token representations as an obstacle to recognizing these combinations.

The method has two connected stages. Compositional Perception maps image patches to a small vocabulary of primitives, using competitive assignments and information exchange to form coherent groups. Generalizing Induction then calibrates spatial relationships while preserving the induced structure and probabilistic meaning. Together, these stages organize the visual representation so that it can better support extrapolation to unseen combinations.

CoGe-GCD fits between an existing backbone and projection head without changing the head or training losses. Across standard benchmarks, it consistently improves accuracy over all classes, estimation of the number of unknown classes, and geometric quality, with marginal computational overhead. The results support compositional structure as a useful addition to multiple category-discovery frameworks.
icml-2026-coge-gcd-reframing-generalized.tldr: CoGe-GCD organizes visual features into reusable primitives and spatial relationships to improve discovery of unfamiliar categories.

paragraphs: Dense associative memories retrieve stored patterns through dynamics that settle at stable points of an energy function. Existing models represent those patterns as vectors. This paper extends the idea to Gaussian probability distributions, making distributions themselves the objects that memory stores and retrieves.

The construction measures differences using the 2-Wasserstein distance and defines an energy that combines contributions from the stored distributions through a log-sum-exp expression. Retrieval aggregates optimal transport maps with Gibbs weights. Its stationary points are self-consistent Wasserstein barycenters: distributional averages that agree with the retrieval rule. This supplies a counterpart to the fixed points used in classical associative memories.

The authors prove exponential storage capacity and quantify retrieval guarantees when inputs are perturbed in Wasserstein distance. They also validate the method on synthetic data and image and text datasets, including CelebA, CIFAR-10, text8, and an NLI corpus. The work provides a mathematical route from vector memories to distributional memories, connecting associative retrieval with representations relevant to generative modeling.
icml-2026-dense-associative-memory-for-g.tldr: This paper extends dense associative memory to Gaussian distributions, with storage-capacity proofs and retrieval guarantees under Wasserstein perturbations.

paragraphs: Tracking entities means remembering how their states change as operations occur. This paper studies how language models handle natural-language problems containing multiple changes, extending investigation beyond entity binding without state updates. It combines observations of model behavior with analysis of the internal mechanisms responsible.

In the studied models and scenarios, the authors find no incremental tracking of world states across tokens or query-relevant states across layers. Instead, the models gather relevant information in parallel at the final token once the query is clear. Analysis of PUT, REMOVE, and MOVE operations reveals how this non-incremental strategy handles a task whose underlying events unfold sequentially.

REMOVE relies on a fragile global suppression tag. That mechanism predicts failure modes, which the authors then confirm through behavioral tests. Nullifying the tag partially addresses the problem. The broader contribution is a feedback loop between behavioral testing and mechanistic explanation: internal findings reveal weaknesses that existing evaluations miss, while observed behavior helps guide hypotheses about the computation.
icml-2026-do-language-models-track-entit.tldr: The studied language models track changing entities through parallel information aggregation, with a fragile removal mechanism that predicts observable failures.

paragraphs: Long inputs make standard attention expensive because its computational cost grows quadratically with sequence length. Combining sparse and full attention can reduce that burden, but existing hybrid strategies usually fix their relative proportions. This leaves the model unable to adjust its computation when different inputs or tasks are more sensitive to sparsity.

Elastic Attention introduces a lightweight router into a pretrained model. The router assigns individual attention heads to different computation modes based on the input. These assignments change the model’s overall sparsity during inference, making the allocation of attention computation responsive to the example being processed. The central design choice is to learn this allocation within the existing model.

The authors report enabling strong performance and efficient inference with 12 hours of training on eight A800 GPUs. Experiments on three long-context benchmarks using widely used language models favor their method. The findings support adaptive sparsity as a practical way to balance attention cost and task performance across varying long-context demands.
icml-2026-elastic-attention-test-time-ad.tldr: Elastic Attention uses an input-dependent router to adjust sparse and full attention across heads for efficient long-context inference.

paragraphs: Euclean addresses the separation between geometry reasoning systems and formal mathematics in Lean. Earlier geometry approaches use specialized languages or custom axiom systems incompatible with standard Mathlib. Formalizing geometry directly in Mathlib requires spelling out assumptions that diagrams often leave implicit, including spatial configuration and non-degeneracy.

The framework carries out four stages: making constraints explicit, anchoring the geometric configuration, mapping the problem into formal statements, and repairing those statements iteratively. This workflow targets native Mathlib formalizations despite its small and rapidly changing geometry infrastructure. The authors use it to construct OMNI-Geometry with 768 competition problems and Numina-Geometry with 177,597 problems.

Human evaluation reports 48.89% TOP1 accuracy and 73.33% TOP5 accuracy. Training Goedel v2 on the formalizations raises proof success from 13.6% to 15.1%, providing evidence that the generated data helps theorem proving. The contribution combines a geometry formalization pipeline with training data intended to support unified verification and model development within Lean.
icml-2026-euclean-automated-geometry-pro.tldr: Euclean formalizes geometry directly in Lean’s Mathlib and produces large training datasets that improve downstream proof success.

paragraphs: Federated learning must choose useful training examples and features while data remains distributed across clients. Communication limits, differing client distributions, and fairness requirements make those choices consequential. This paper argues that selecting examples and features separately overlooks their interaction, especially in noisy data with many dimensions.

FedGCUR formulates both choices through generalized CUR decomposition, connecting the selection of rows and columns in a data matrix. Its federated column-pivoted QR routine, FedCPQR, handles the feature side, while individual silos select rows. This gives the two selection tasks a shared mathematical framework instead of treating each as an independent preprocessing decision.

The authors prove that FedCPQR returns exactly the same decomposition as centralized column-pivoted QR and establish an upper bound on FedGCUR’s reconstruction error. Experiments on tabular and vision tasks show strong downstream accuracy and CUR reconstruction quality against representative selection baselines. The theoretical and empirical results connect distributed selection to both faithful data reconstruction and useful model training.
icml-2026-federated-data-and-feature-sel.tldr: FedGCUR jointly selects data and features in federated learning, with centralized-equivalent QR decomposition and a reconstruction-error bound.

paragraphs: Extreme-weather diagnosis requires interpreting anomalous signals through several reasoning steps, choosing tools as the investigation develops, and applying expert judgment. The paper argues that progress in weather forecasting does not by itself resolve these diagnostic demands. Existing agent systems also struggle to integrate specialist knowledge and evaluate complicated reasoning workflows.

HVR-Met is a multi-agent diagnostic system built around a repeated cycle of proposing a hypothesis, verifying it, and revising the plan. Expert meteorological knowledge is integrated into this process. The cycle gives the system a way to revisit its interpretation of unusual weather signals as verification produces evidence, supporting iterative investigation during extreme events.

The authors also introduce a benchmark focused on atomic subtasks, addressing the need to evaluate fine-grained parts of a diagnostic workflow. Their experiments report strong performance in complex diagnostic scenarios. The combined contribution is a specialist reasoning architecture and an evaluation approach that examines the smaller tasks involved in carrying out an extended meteorological diagnosis.
icml-2026-hvr-met-a-hypothesis-verificat.tldr: HVR-Met combines meteorological expertise with repeated hypothesis testing and replanning for complex extreme-weather diagnosis.

paragraphs: Discrete diffusion language models generate text through repeated denoising steps that can update positions in parallel. Evaluating them is difficult because errors can come from either the learned denoiser or the sampling procedure. Ordinary evaluation combines these sources, making it hard to tell whether better denoising would fix an observed sampling problem.

The paper builds a controlled framework that replaces the learned denoiser with an exact posterior from a Hidden Markov Model based on a known Markov chain. Removing denoiser approximation error exposes errors introduced by the sampling dynamics themselves. This lets the authors assess whether the sampler reproduces the intended distribution even with perfect denoising information.

In this setting, few-step samplers remain distributionally incorrect. Transition-level discrepancies disappear only as the number of sampling steps approaches the sequence length. Improvements in negative log-likelihood, generative perplexity, or MAUVE also do not imply correct sampling. The findings distinguish better evaluation scores from faithful reproduction of a model’s intended probability distribution.
icml-2026-is-your-diffusion-sampler-actu.tldr: An exact-denoiser evaluation shows that few-step discrete diffusion sampling can distort the intended distribution despite improved standard metrics.

paragraphs: Importance-Weighted Neural Processes use multiple latent particles to model task uncertainty and tightly approximate marginal log-likelihood. This paper identifies an imbalance in their training: particles that already assign high likelihood receive dominant gradient signals. Lower-likelihood regions receive less attention, contributing to weak tail-risk generation and unstable rapid adaptation.

Order-Statistics Aligned Neural Processes address this imbalance by sorting particles into separate difficulty bins using order statistics. The authors derive a regularized worst-case optimization framework and align loss reduction across those strata. This gives difficult latent regions a structured role in training. It targets the trade-off seen with robust objectives such as CVaR, which can improve risk handling while reducing average performance.

The paper provides a computationally efficient implementation pipeline and reports extensive experiments showing improved tail-risk robustness alongside maintained or improved average results. These findings support balancing learning across latent difficulty levels as a route to more stable probabilistic meta-learning. The reported benefit includes both reliability in difficult regions and preservation of typical performance.
icml-2026-latent-space-robust-optimizati.tldr: OS-NPs balance learning across latent-particle difficulty groups, improving tail-risk robustness while maintaining or improving average performance in experiments.

paragraphs: Learning to rank can be framed as assigning probability to an entire ordering of items. Directly computing and optimizing that probability becomes intractable as the number of possible permutations grows factorially. This paper seeks a manageable training objective that still represents the structure of the complete list.

The Full-Order Bound is a lower bound on the probability of an observed ordering. It uses a subset of ordering constraints that factorizes across items while preserving full-order structure and invariance to order reversal. Under the stated assumption of log-concave latent densities, tightening the bound over latent cut points becomes a convex inner problem. A safe-region gradient ascent procedure solves that problem during training.

Experiments on synthetic tasks and large learning-to-rank benchmarks show improved full-list ordering metrics, with competitive NDCG performance. An optional variant aligned with the evaluation metric recovers NDCG gains. The results show how a tractable approximation to whole-order probability can support ranking objectives while retaining a meaningful connection to complete-list correctness.
icml-2026-learning-to-rank-by-directly-o.tldr: The Full-Order Bound makes whole-list ranking probabilities tractable to optimize and improves full-order metrics in experiments.

paragraphs: MemCast treats time-series forecasting as reasoning informed by accumulated experience. The paper targets a gap in existing language-model forecasters: they can make effective predictions without explicitly organizing past experience or supporting continued evolution. Its learning-to-memory framework extracts reusable knowledge from the training set and stores it hierarchically.

The memory has three complementary forms. Prediction results become historical patterns, inference trajectories become guidance about reasoning, and temporal features become general laws. At inference time, patterns guide the reasoning process, reasoning guidance helps select trajectories, and general laws provide criteria for reflective revision. Each memory layer therefore has a distinct role in producing and reconsidering a forecast.

A dynamic confidence adaptation strategy updates confidence in individual memory entries without leaking the test-set distribution. Across multiple datasets, the authors report consistent improvements over previous methods. The results support explicitly organized experience as a useful resource for forecasting, with adaptation occurring through confidence in remembered knowledge as well as its use during reasoning.
icml-2026-memcast-memory-driven-time-ser.tldr: MemCast improves time-series forecasting by organizing training experience into memories that guide, select, and revise reasoning.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding speeds up language-model generation by having a smaller model propose tokens for a larger model to verify. Standard implementations run these stages sequentially, so drafting remains part of the waiting time before verification can proceed. MineDraft addresses this scheduling bottleneck by overlapping work across request batches.

The framework maintains two batches. While the target model verifies proposals for one batch, the draft model prepares proposals for the other. This batch-parallel organization is designed to hide drafting latency behind verification. The paper’s theoretical analysis finds substantially greater efficiency for parallel speculative decoding than for the standard sequential approach.

Experiments report throughput improvements of up to 75% and end-to-end latency improvements of up to 39% over standard speculative decoding. The authors also implement MineDraft as a vLLM plugin, demonstrating integration with an inference system used for serving models. The contribution shows how coordinating the drafting and verification stages across requests can improve both service capacity and response time.
icml-2026-minedraft-a-framework-for-batc.tldr: MineDraft overlaps drafting and verification across two request batches, improving throughput and latency over standard speculative decoding.

paragraphs: Cooperative multi-agent planning becomes difficult because combinations of agent actions grow exponentially. Monte Carlo Tree Search can spend its limited budget exploring this enormous space without finding useful coordination. NonZero makes selection more manageable through a low-dimensional nonlinear representation and a surrogate that guides candidate exploration.

Its proposal rule explicitly considers interactions. Changes by one agent are ranked by predicted benefit, while changes by two agents receive a mixed-difference score that can expose coordination benefits even when neither agent can improve alone. The authors formulate candidate selection as a bandit problem over local deviations and derive the NonUCT proposal rule.

NonUCT has a sublinear local-regret guarantee for reaching approximate graph-local optima without enumerating all joint actions. This guarantee concerns local search quality. Experiments on MatGame, SMAC, and SMACv2 show better sample efficiency and final performance than strong model-based and model-free baselines under matched search budgets. The findings support directing exploration toward interactions that individual action changes would miss.
icml-2026-nonzero-interaction-guided-exp.tldr: NonZero guides multi-agent tree search toward useful individual and paired action changes, improving exploration without enumerating joint actions.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning uses a learned dynamics model to improve sample efficiency. A mismatch arises because that model learns from experience collected by older policies while the current policy continues changing. Prediction error can fall overall yet remain large in regions important to current decisions, producing unstable policy updates.

The paper analyzes this issue over a finite horizon. It separates the policy performance gap into global model error, policy-induced distribution shift, and effects from the mixture of historical policies. The analysis shows why minimizing aggregate prediction error alone is insufficient for stable optimization. It motivates directing more model-training effort toward transitions where predictions remain inaccurate.

Prioritized Model Experience Replay implements that idea through a lightweight replay mechanism that favors high-error transitions. This implicitly emphasizes policy-relevant regions without explicitly estimating distances between policies and fits into Dyna-style frameworks. On MuJoCo benchmarks, the authors report greater stability, faster convergence, and improved sample efficiency. The contribution links a diagnosis of model-training mismatch to a practical change in experience selection.
icml-2026-prioritized-model-experience-r.tldr: PMER prioritizes high-error transitions when training dynamics models, improving stability and sample efficiency in model-based reinforcement learning experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies networks whose activation functions are trainable, low-degree rational functions. It compares their representational efficiency with a broad collection of fixed activations, including ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, and several modern smooth alternatives. The main question is how much network size is needed to approximate one family using the other.

For an error target epsilon, the authors show that rational-activation networks can uniformly approximate networks using the studied standard activations on compact domains with size overhead polynomial in log log of one over epsilon. In the reverse direction, approximation requires at least order log of one over epsilon parameters in the worst case. The resulting exponential separation extends to complete networks, gated activations, and transformer-style nonlinearities.

The paper also reports that rational activations fit into standard architectures and training pipelines, matching or outperforming fixed activations with identical architectures and optimizers. These empirical findings complement the approximation results. The theoretical advantage concerns representation and parameter requirements, while the practical comparisons show that trainable rational nonlinearities can also work effectively in ordinary training setups.
icml-2026-rational-neural-networks-have-.tldr: Trainable rational activations offer provable approximation-efficiency advantages and match or outperform fixed activations in the reported practical comparisons.

paragraphs: Reconstructing moving scenes with shiny surfaces requires estimating where reflected rays travel and modeling how materials produce reflections. ReflFlow addresses both challenges in a framework for rendering dynamic specular scenes. Its design connects the representation of changing geometry to the computation of reflection directions.

The method uses a residual, material-augmented 2D Gaussian Splatting representation to model geometry and material properties together. A Dynamic Environment Gaussian and a hybrid rendering pipeline then separate diffuse and specular components. Rasterization and ray tracing support physically informed synthesis of the reflective component. This decomposition gives geometry, materials, and reflection rendering distinct but connected roles.

Training proceeds from coarse to fine to improve optimization stability and encourage a physically meaningful separation of the components. On dynamic-scene benchmarks, the authors report quantitative and qualitative improvements over prior methods, including sharper and more realistic reflections in complex changing environments. The results support combining geometry-guided reflection computation with a rendering pipeline that explicitly accounts for specular appearance.
icml-2026-reflflow-learning-geometry-gui.tldr: ReflFlow combines dynamic geometry and material modeling with hybrid rendering to produce sharper, more realistic reflections in moving scenes.

paragraphs: Self-play alignment treats language-model preference optimization as a two-player game. This paper examines how regularization relative to a reference policy affects that process. Such regularization matters for controlling over-optimization, but the authors argue that its role in self-play has received insufficient attention.

Regularized Self-Play Policy Optimization provides a common framework for earlier methods and allows regularizers to be added as interchangeable components. It preserves convergence to a Nash equilibrium of the corresponding regularized game. This connects the practical choice of regularization to a defined game-theoretic target while supporting comparisons among different strategies.

With appropriate regularizers, RSPO raises AlpacaEval-2 length-controlled win rates from 28.5% to 35.4% for Mistral-7B, 38.77% to 43.66% for LLaMA-8B, and 50.54% to 51.83% for Gemma-2B over unregularized SPPO. The authors also report consistently stronger results on Arena-Hard, MT-Bench, ArmoRM, and response diversity. These findings show that regularization choices can materially improve self-play alignment across several base models and evaluation settings.
icml-2026-rspo-regularized-self-play-ali.tldr: RSPO adds interchangeable regularizers to self-play alignment, preserving game-equilibrium convergence and improving reported preference and diversity results.

paragraphs: SAQNN addresses a foundational question in quantum machine learning: which functions can a quantum neural network represent, and how large must the representation be? The authors propose a constructive model and prove that it has the universal approximation property for square-integrable functions. Within that function class, it can achieve arbitrarily accurate approximation.

The model also supports changing function bases. This makes the construction adaptable to different numerical approximation and machine-learning settings by allowing different building blocks for representing a target function. The result therefore combines an expressivity theorem with flexibility in the representation used to realize that expressivity.

The paper establishes asymptotic circuit-size advantages over the best classical feed-forward neural networks and optimal parameter complexity for approximating Sobolev functions under the L2 norm. These are resource statements tied to the specified approximation setting and error measure. Together, the results strengthen the theoretical foundation for quantum neural networks by addressing both the range of representable functions and the resources needed to approximate them.
icml-2026-saqnn-spectral-adaptive-quantu.tldr: SAQNN is a constructive quantum neural network with universal approximation and provable resource advantages in specified function-approximation settings.

paragraphs: Language models can lack knowledge in specialized domains where training data is scarce. SPA studies whether generating large amounts of synthetic data with a small collection of carefully designed prompts can provide an effective knowledge-injection baseline. The approach focuses on prompt quality and augmentation scale.

Systematic comparisons find that SPA outperforms several strong baselines. The analysis identifies two reasons more elaborate approaches can lose their advantage. Reinforcement-learning-based augmentation may use tokens more efficiently at small scale, but suffers from diversity collapse as generation scales, producing diminishing returns. Multi-stage prompting can outperform simpler augmentation, yet that advantage can disappear when the simpler method’s prompts are carefully tuned.

The findings suggest that complexity alone is an unreliable guide to knowledge-injection effectiveness. Prompt design and the diversity of generated material matter when assessing a method at scale. SPA offers a straightforward reference point for future comparisons, showing that carefully engineered prompts combined with large-scale generation can be competitive without a more involved augmentation procedure.
icml-2026-spa-a-simple-but-tough-to-beat.tldr: SPA shows that carefully tuned prompts and large-scale synthetic augmentation can outperform more elaborate knowledge-injection methods.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes two ways language-model representations can deteriorate over long contexts. Excessive homogenization can erase distinctions between representations, while excessive isolation can disconnect parts of the context. Spectral analysis identifies a trade-off between efficient information mixing, measured by spectral gap, and information capacity, measured by effective rank.

The Topologically Regularized Side-Path adds a route for token interaction without changing core attention. It uses a parameter-free Triangular Box mechanism controlled by a lightweight gate that accounts for sequence length. Nearby coupling helps preserve effective rank, while longer-range propagation supports mixing. These components aim to balance information exchange with preservation of distinct representations.

Experiments show improvements on general-capability and long-context benchmarks. On NoLiMa at eight times the training length, TRSP retains 83% accuracy, exceeding the Differential Transformer and Gated Attention by approximately 30 and 50 percentage points, respectively. The results support the proposed spectral balance as a useful architectural intervention for maintaining performance when context length grows beyond training conditions.
icml-2026-the-devil-is-in-the-spectrum-m.tldr: TRSP adds a lightweight side path that balances information mixing and representation capacity, improving reported long-context performance.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers often include extra tokens for aggregation or artifact reduction, but those tokens usually lack a clear semantic organization. XTRA asks whether dedicated extra tokens can instead learn separate meaningful parts of an image, such as heads, bodies, and legs, without explicit supervision for those parts.

The framework adds factor tokens and trains them with a Minimum Volume Constraint intended to encourage disentanglement. That constraint alone can cause token collapse, so XTRA also uses multi-stage aggregation to promote semantically pure components. The combination addresses both separation between factors and the need for those factors to retain useful, distinct content.

On ImageNet-1K, XTRA reports an 8.4-fold improvement over DINOv2 in the SEPIN@1 disentanglement measure. It also improves KNN accuracy by 5.8% and linear-probe accuracy by 2.3%, as reported in the abstract. These results suggest that organizing extra tokens into semantic factors can improve representation quality alongside disentanglement, making the added structure useful for more than interpreting image components.
icml-2026-the-extra-tokens-matter-disent.tldr: XTRA trains extra Vision Transformer tokens to represent distinct semantic parts, improving disentanglement and representation quality on ImageNet-1K.

paragraphs: Visual reasoning systems often express intermediate steps in text, which can lose visual information and make the interaction between perception and reasoning unstable or expensive. LDPVR approaches reasoning as a repeated exchange between latent thought and visual evidence. Explicit textual states become progressively simpler as latent transitions guide their refinement.

The framework models this process as a Markov chain of recursive state simplification. Its Interleaved Latent Grounding component uses latent semantic intent to retrieve detailed visual evidence. This allows the system to reduce uncertainty before settling on a simplified textual state, connecting each refinement to information from the image.

Training follows three stages: supervised fine-tuning, distillation between latent and textual representations, and reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization. Across six multimodal reasoning benchmarks, the authors report improved reasoning accuracy while maintaining low inference latency. The findings support an iterative relationship between visual grounding and internal reasoning, with concise textual states emerging through refinement rather than carrying the entire reasoning process.
icml-2026-thinking-in-latent-space-progr.tldr: LDPVR alternates latent reasoning with targeted visual grounding to simplify textual states, improving accuracy while maintaining low inference latency.

paragraphs: Generalized zero-shot learning must recognize both categories seen during training and categories absent from training. Models often favor familiar categories when these groups appear together at test time. PUFE addresses this bias by treating inference as a positive-unlabeled learning problem, with seen categories supplying positives and the mixed test data remaining unlabeled.

The framework builds a classifier in semantic space using a network with two output heads. Maximum likelihood estimation jointly learns the probability of belonging to a seen class and the propensity for labeling. The classifier then identifies high-confidence pseudo-instances, which guide adaptive calibration of semantic prototypes so that those prototypes better match the underlying test distribution.

PUFE operates as a plug-and-play post-processing framework and improves diverse generalized zero-shot learning baselines across multiple architectural families. Experiments report gains of up to 11.2 percentage points in harmonic mean performance. The results support combining an explicit estimate of seen-class membership with prototype adjustment to reduce the imbalance between recognition of familiar and unfamiliar categories.
icml-2026-when-generalized-zero-shot-lea.tldr: PUFE reduces seen-class bias in generalized zero-shot learning through positive-unlabeled classification and adaptive semantic-prototype calibration.
